extracted.intended_audience: instructors teaching undergraduate (and advanced high-school) discrete mathematics courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing, selecting, and implementing classroom-tested projects, historical modules, exercises, and pedagogical practices for discrete mathematics courses (including materials, timing, student activities, and proof pedagogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project format: summary, notes, references, worksheets, solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The format for each is a summary, notes to the instructor, references, student worksheets (often mixed with explanatory handouts), and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each project should include these components so instructors can quickly understand the goal (summary), implementation issues (notes), sources (references), student-facing material (worksheets/handouts), and instructor-facing answers (solutions). Solutions may also contain extension questions or research-worthy problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotated table of contents with summaries and time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The table of contents is annotated with a summary of each project or article and, for the classroom projects, how many 50-minute periods an instructor might dedicate to the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide per-project short summaries and explicit estimates of class time (in 50-minute periods) to aid instructors in planning and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate classroom-tested status and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should be classroom-tested and reflect implementation by instructors from a variety of institutions (college, high school, new instructors to experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that materials were used in real classes, include notes about typical student responses, common difficulties, and origins (who tested it) so instructors can trust and adapt the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give explicit class-period/time guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For each activity give an estimate of how many class periods (generally 50-minute periods) the activity requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include guidance such as 'one to two class periods', 'two or more class periods', or 'less than one class period per worksheet' so instructors can schedule appropriately and adapt pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes to instructor with implementation strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete 'Notes for the instructor' including suggested class flow, group sizes, in-class vs. homework split, instructor prompts, and common scaffolding tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: divide students into groups of 3–4, walk around observing groups, suggest simplifying parameters for struggling teams, require polished written explanations as homework, conduct whole-class critique sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include exercises, solutions, and extension/open-ended questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should include exercises and solutions; some should include open-ended questions and extension questions suitable for student research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer both routine exercises (with solutions) and extension problems to engage advanced students or provide options for student research projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: State intended student audience and course role
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what students the activity serves and the course role (e.g., mathematics majors, computer science majors, general education students, intro vs. advanced topic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note whether an activity introduces proof writing, extends common topics, or is intended for lab/experimental sessions so instructors can match activities to their enrollment and course goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a diversity of modalities: manipulatives, technology, programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials should leverage varied modalities where appropriate—manipulatives (integer rods, strings, pipes), technology (graphing calculators, CAS), and programming/coding extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific examples of manipulatives and technological tools, and give suggestions for coding extensions or calculator worksheets to connect discrete topics to computation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and align projects topically with common texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Classroom projects are ordered topically (the book follows Susanna Epp’s Discrete Mathematics with Applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align project ordering and topic headings with common course texts or curricular sequences so instructors can insert projects at appropriate points in a syllabus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide variants and multiple difficulty levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should offer variants and a range of difficulty so they can be used for introductory treatment or for more advanced exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include simpler starting cases (e.g., start with 6 tokens instead of 9), harder extensions, and alternate formulations that can be revisited later in the course to deepen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical modules: original sources, chronology, and instructor notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical projects should draw from original sources, be arranged chronologically, and include a combined introduction explaining how to use them in class plus instructor notes and exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context linking original historical texts to classroom exercises, suggest student activities working from the sources, and indicate prerequisite knowledge for each module.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit learning goals: proof-writing and clear exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities should be designed to develop specific skills such as discovering strategies and giving a 'careful written explanation' or learning to write proofs clearly for a given audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set concrete writing tasks (e.g., a full paragraph explaining a strategy to a roommate), require that students aim proofs at an appropriate audience, and structure follow-up critique sessions to improve exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use puzzles and exploratory problems to motivate proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose puzzles (e.g., pile splitting to introduce strong induction) that naturally motivate the need for specific proof methods and recursive thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present puzzles, let students conjecture from examples, then introduce the formal proof technique (e.g., strong induction) as the tool to justify the conjecture; provide a worked proof as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide scripts/templates for proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: During the induction (and other proof) phase, present a template or 'script' for a correct induction argument and require students to follow it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit templates for base case, inductive hypothesis, and inductive step; require students to use the script to build confidence and logical structure in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning structure: group work, play, and instructor observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ active learning: divide students into small groups, have them play or manipulate materials, and the instructor should circulate and intervene when groups become frustrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes suggesting simplified parameters for struggling groups, ensuring key insights are reached within a target time (e.g., 25 minutes), and offering competitive play or challenges between groups to maintain engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor-led critique and peer review of student proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in-class critique sessions where student-written proofs are displayed and the class critiques exposition, pointing out unclear parts while the instructor moderates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select volunteer proofs for board presentation, allocate ~20 minutes for critique, and guide students to identify unclear exposition and correctness issues; encourage students to show drafts to non-expert peers to test clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting proofs as formative assessment with structured feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Require students to rewrite proofs until they are correct and provide structured feedback on drafts (method, argument, English composition), especially where class size allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hagelgans' concrete suggestions: have students submit double-spaced, word-processed drafts; write comments in pencil; comment on appropriateness of proof method and argument; if valid, comment on English; mention good points; hold conferences with weak students; consider whole-class discussion of selected drafts or peer commenting exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate proof via experiments, counterexamples, and 'scientific debate'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experimental labs and contentious statements where reasonable people might disagree (or generate counterexamples) to motivate the need for rigorous proof and validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a three-step 'scientific debate' process: (1) students produce statements without immediate evaluation, (2) students discuss and vote, supporting positions with arguments/counterexamples, (3) validated statements become theorems while incorrect ones are recorded with counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Moore or modified Moore method for deep theorem-proving practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In Moore-style courses, give students definitions and an ordered list of statements to prove or disprove without consulting external sources, emphasizing student presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broader applicability, adapt the method: include elementary exercises on definitions, provide hints during office hours, and give periodic exams with prepared proofs for review before tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use laboratory/experimental sessions to bridge discovery and formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate weekly laboratory sessions for exploration/experimentation (often with the computer) alongside a conventional exposition to help students generate conjectures and then move to analytic proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory activities should produce data/examples that prompt conjecture formation; follow with guided formalization and proof-writing in class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly address process and affective issues in mathematical discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the psychological aspects of problem-solving (ups and downs, persistence, switching strategies) and teach heuristics for structuring inquiry (imagine objects, try counterexamples, attempt contradictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples (e.g., Wiles' Fermat narrative) and research findings (Schoenfeld) to show problem-solving habits: persistence combined with readiness to change approach; encourage reflection on how solutions were found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select projects that connect to real applications to show relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose activities that illustrate real-world connections (chemistry—benzenoids and matchings, bioinformatics, information storage, typesetting/TEX, data compression) to motivate students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit ties between discrete math concepts and applications (e.g., encryption, engineering) to underscore the practical importance of careful proof and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide short exercises/worksheets for quick technology-based exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short worksheets (e.g., calculator activities) that can be completed in less than one class period to demonstrate concepts using graphing calculators and computer algebra systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design these worksheets to explore modular arithmetic, floor/ceiling functions, growth of functions, and how technology assists with pattern recognition and proof ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include open-ended, research-like projects for advanced engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer 'very open' projects that ask students to define notions (e.g., graph complexity) and explore them, suitable for two or more class periods and potential student research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide guidance and background material but leave room for student-defined inquiries and longer-term projects across multiple sessions.
